markdown:
## In Plain English

This case asks whether a federal privacy law called the Video Privacy Protection Act protects someone who subscribes to a sports website’s online newsletter but also watches videos on that site. It matters to regular people because it could decide how broadly the law applies when a company shares information about what videos someone watched with a social media platform.

## The Backstory

Michael Salazar filed a class action lawsuit — a lawsuit brought by one person on behalf of a group of people with similar claims — against Paramount Global, doing business as 247Sports. He sued in a federal trial court in Tennessee in September 2022.

Salazar alleged that he subscribed to 247Sports’ online newsletter in 2022 and watched videos on the site while logged into his Facebook account. He also alleged that Paramount used a Facebook tracking tool called a Pixel, which sent Facebook information about the videos he watched, linked to his Facebook ID, without his consent.

Salazar claimed this violated the Video Privacy Protection Act, a federal law that limits when a “video tape service provider” — a company in the business of delivering audiovisual materials — may knowingly share “personally identifiable information” about a “consumer.” In this case, the personally identifiable information alleged was Salazar’s Facebook ID linked to his video-watching history.

The trial court dismissed Salazar’s case in July 2023. It said he was not a “consumer” under the law because he had not subscribed to audiovisual goods or services. The court noted that Salazar had not alleged that the newsletter itself was audiovisual content or that he could access videos only through the newsletter.

The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit agreed and affirmed the dismissal in April 2025. The full Sixth Circuit declined to reconsider the case in May 2025.

Salazar then asked the Supreme Court to review the case by filing a petition for a writ of certiorari — a request asking the Court to hear the case. The Supreme Court agreed to review the case in January 2026. The parties filed their main Supreme Court briefs, and the case was argued on October 14, 2026.

## What Each Side Argues

### Michael Salazar’s arguments

- The Video Privacy Protection Act says a “consumer” includes a “subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” Salazar argues that the phrase “goods or services” is not limited to videos or other audiovisual content.
- Salazar says he subscribed to Paramount’s online newsletter, which is a good or service from a company that both lower courts assumed is a video tape service provider.
- He argues that the law says “any consumer,” and that courts should not add extra limits that do not appear in the statute.
- Salazar’s petition says there is a disagreement among lower federal appeals courts — a circuit split — about whether a person must subscribe to audiovisual goods or services to be covered by the law.
- He says the Sixth Circuit’s reading is wrong because it narrows the law’s definition of “consumer” and makes some statutory language unnecessary.
- The petition also says both lower courts assumed Paramount is a video tape service provider and that the information disclosed was personally identifiable information. The only disputed question, in Salazar’s view, is whether he qualifies as a “consumer.”

### Paramount Global’s arguments

- The full text of Paramount’s Supreme Court brief is not included in the provided excerpts. But the lower-court opinion included in the filings shows Paramount’s position: to be a “consumer” under the Video Privacy Protection Act, a person must subscribe to goods or services related to audiovisual content, not just any product or service offered by the company.
- Paramount’s position, as reflected in the lower-court decision, is that Salazar’s newsletter subscription did not make him a consumer because the newsletter was not shown to be audiovisual content.
- The lower courts also emphasized that Salazar did not allege that he could access videos only through the newsletter or that the newsletter itself delivered audiovisual materials.
- Paramount’s broader position, as reflected in the lower-court opinion, is that the law’s context and its definition of “video tape service provider” limit who counts as a protected consumer.

## Where the Case Stands

The Supreme Court granted review on January 26, 2026. Salazar filed his merits brief on April 17, 2026. Paramount filed its merits brief on June 23, 2026. Salazar filed a reply on July 23, 2026. The docket also lists 14 friend-of-the-court briefs, called amicus briefs, filed by outside groups or individuals.

The case was argued before the Supreme Court on October 14, 2026. Joshua I. Hammack argued for Salazar, and Paul D. Clement argued for Paramount.

The provided docket does not show a decision. The case remains pending after argument, and the Court has not yet issued an opinion in the materials provided.

## Legal Terms Explained

- **Writ of certiorari**: A request asking the Supreme Court to review a lower court’s decision. The Court grants these requests only in selected cases.
- **Circuit split**: A disagreement among different federal appeals courts about what a law means.
- **Class action**: A lawsuit in which one person sues on behalf of a larger group of people who have similar claims.
- **Personally identifiable information**: Information that can identify a person and connect that person to specific video materials or services. In this case, the alleged information was a Facebook ID linked to video-watching history.
- **Video tape service provider**: A company in the business of delivering audiovisual materials. The statute uses this older term, and the parties in this case assumed Paramount fits that description.
